"Pharma X Ltd." is a pharmaceutical company with a board of directors. An investigation reveals that the company has been peddling unregistered opioids "Real" at a local market through an unauthorised agent, which is an offence under the Health Professions Regulatory Bodies Act 2013, Act 857. Consequently, the company and all its directors are charged by the Pharmacy Council. During the disciplinary proceedings, the following facts are established:

i) Director A (the CEO): Personally, approved the plan and authorized the funds for the illegal peddling scheme.
ii) Director B (a non-executive director): Was completely unaware of the scheme. She successfully proves in the hearings that she had no knowledge of the operation and did not consent to it.

Case: suspected deep vein thrombosis

A patient with obesity and chronic hypertension, taking amlodipine and bendrofluazide, develops unilateral leg swelling after prolonged travel from Accra to Kintampo. The clinical team suspects and confirms a provoked deep vein thrombosis and considers enoxaparin, rivaroxaban, and warfarin while assessing renal function and treatment duration.

Case II: the Bagre Dam flooding

The Bagre Dam spillage in August 2024 led to flooding in Ghana's Upper East Region, contaminating water sources and increasing the risk of cholera outbreaks. The White Volta River broke its banks, submerging farmlands and houses. The National Disaster Management Organisation reported affected areas in Binduri, Bawku West, and Talensi districts, with three deaths including a five-year-old child. A Regional Health Director constituted a team, including a pharmacist, to address the public health and pharmacy-service needs.

Case I: illegal activities at an OTC medicine shop

A complaint was lodged at the Office of the Registrar of the Pharmacy Council about an over-the-counter medicine shop. The facility sold antihypertensives, antidiabetics, vaccines kept outside the fridge, pethidine, and morphine, and employed a nurse to administer injections. Council officers found the signage “ECODIN CHEMIST”, evidence of injections, invoices showing pethidine and morphine supply from a wholesale pharmacy, doubts about product registration, and absenteeism by the wholesale pharmacy’s Superintendent Pharmacist.

Case II: Pharm Kwame Ansah at Medifast Pharmacy

Pharm Kwame Ansah is the superintendent pharmacist at Medifast Pharmacy in Accra. A mother requests azithromycin for her five-year-old son without a prescription. Pharm Ansah refuses and refers her. Later, a valid prescription for amoxicillin is brought, but he dispenses it without checking the child’s documented penicillin allergy or counselling. The child suffers anaphylaxis. An investigation later finds that Pharm Ansah diverted controlled medicines for personal profit and overcharged indigent patients while claiming a government subsidy.

Case I: PharmaSol manufacturing deviations

PharmaSol Ltd. is a licensed pharmaceutical manufacturing company producing OTC medicines, including Parasol 500 mg tablets. During batch production, several deviations occurred, including shortened mixing time, high particulate counts, batch-record entries written in pencil and later overwritten in pen, an out-of-specification assay result of 92.2%, and an unauthorized repeat result of 96.8%.

Case II: The Silent River

Kwame, a 42-year-old farmer living downstream from a galamsey site, presents with metallic taste, tremors, abdominal pain, frothy urine, memory lapses, irritability, bluish-purple discoloration along the gum line, acral peeling, elevated serum creatinine, and proteinuria. Upstream miners use liquid silver (mercury) to amalgamate gold and cyanide for heap leaching. River water is used for drinking and cooking.

A 32-year-old female presented to the clinic with a skin infection on the left shin

Research Question: How does the incidence of chemotherapy-induced neutropenia differ 
between patients receiving Drug X and those receiving standard chemotherapy alone? 
Methods:
A total of 1,000 patients with stage II or III breast cancer were enrolled from an oncology 
clinic. A total of 
500 patients received Drug X in addition to standard chemotherapy, and 500 received 
standard chemotherapy only. Patients with a prior history of severe neutropenia were 
excluded. Participants were followed for 24 months to record new cases of neutropenia. 
Results:
The follow-up rate was 75% for the Drug X group and 25% for the standard-therapy group. 
During followup, 20 cases of neutropenia occurred in the Drug X group and 10 cases in the 
standard-therapy group. 
Conclusion:
The study concludes that patients receiving Drug X have a higher risk of developing 
neutropenia compared to those on standard chemotherapy alone.
